## Conclusion

**No — the best available evidence shows ivermectin does not reduce COVID-19 mortality.** Early observational studies and small trials suggested a possible benefit, but this was not confirmed by large, well-designed randomized controlled trials, and much of the early positive evidence came from flawed or fraudulent studies.

The two largest, most rigorous RCTs — the Brazilian **TOGETHER trial** (published in *NEJM*) and the U.S. **ACTIV-6 trial** (published in *JAMA*) — both found no significant reduction in hospitalization or death among outpatients treated with ivermectin compared with placebo. A comprehensive 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 33 RCTs (n=10,489 patients), published in *Heliyon/Cell Press*, similarly concluded that ivermectin "did not have an effect in reducing the risk of mortality in patients with COVID-19." Other meta-analyses reach similar conclusions, noting that any apparent mortality benefit seen in earlier pooled analyses (e.g., a 2021 *Pharmacotherapy* paper) was based on low-certainty evidence and studies that were later retracted or found to include fraudulent data.

Major health authorities — the FDA, WHO, and the Infectious Diseases Society of America — do not recommend ivermectin for COVID-19 treatment outside of clinical trials, based on this body of evidence.

**Bottom line:** Based on large randomized trials and recent systematic reviews, ivermectin does not lower the risk of death from COVID-19.
